judgements.reason: The advisory's defect is one concrete flaw: model-supplied `host`/`proxy` spread into the options bag that carries the server's CMA PAT, so the credential goes to an attacker endpoint. F-001 asserts an architectural condition instead - a single agent holding private data, untrusted ingestion and an outbound channel with no provenance marking - and cites the host/proxy lines only as one of three legs, explicitly deferring the concrete defect to F-002. Same files, but the claimed defect is the design of the server, not the unvalidated parameter.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether the advisory is read as covering the enabling architecture or strictly the parameter flow; as written the advisory fixes the parameters, not the trifecta, and F-001's own recommendation (split servers, degrade privilege) would not be accepted as the fix for it.

judgements.reason: Identical mechanism and identical consequence: both say exportSpace/importSpace declare `host` and `proxy` as ordinary model-supplied parameters, both are spread via `{ ...args, managementToken }` into the job options at exportSpace.ts:134-140 / importSpace.ts:111-115, and both conclude the operator's CMA token is delivered to a model-chosen endpoint. The finding additionally names `hostDelivery`, `rawProxy` and `headers`, which is a superset of the advisory's parameters on the same code path, not a different defect.

Same two files and the same `{ ...args }` spread, but a different parameter pair (`spaceId`/`environmentId` instead of `host`/`proxy`) reaching a different effect: the operation targets a space the operator never configured, a cross-space read/write inside the organization, rather than diverting the credentialed request off-platform. Fixing the host and proxy parameters leaves this untouched.

The advisory's sink is the CMA client's baseURL, reached through `host`; F-004's sink is the local filesystem, reached through `exportDir`/`contentFile`/`errorLogFile`/`assetsDirectory`/`config`, with the effect being an arbitrary file write outside the working directory. Same files and same root pattern of unfiltered model arguments, different parameters and a different consequence.

The end state overlaps - CMA traffic bearing the operator's token is redirected to a host the attacker chose - but the mechanism and the place are different: dotenv.config() with no explicit path in packages/mcp-server/src/config/env.ts picks up a .env from the process working directory, with no LLM, no tool call and no argument spreading involved, and the advisory's fix (stop trusting args.host in the two job tools) does not close it.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether the advisory is scoped to the attacker-controlled-host effect in general or to the LLM-controlled tool argument. Its title, summary and root-cause excerpt all name the tool args, so the shared effect is not enough to make it the same defect.

judgements.reason: F-006 is about the missing authorization boundary around the same two tools: registeredTool.disable() is undone by a handler the model itself can call, and no human sees the literal arguments. That is an absent control, not the unvalidated `host`/`proxy` flow the advisory describes; the finding treats the advisory's defect as a precondition it fails to bound.

Same two tools, but the defect is the direction of the defaults - `skipContentUpdates`/`skipContentPublishing` false and `skipRoles`/`skipWebhooks` false - producing overwrite-and-publish over live content and roles/webhooks in the dump. Nothing here concerns the destination host or the credential's transport, so it is an adjacent defect in the same schemas.

Both concern credentials in exportSpace.ts, but in opposite directions: the advisory is the server's own PAT being sent to a model-chosen host, while F-008 is a different credential (`deliveryToken`, exportSpace.ts:95) entering the model's context and the transcript as a tool argument, with no exploit path asserted. Same file and same schema, different credential and different exposure.

The advisory is about model-controlled transport parameters carrying the PAT out of the two migration tools; F-009 is about tool identity hygiene in packages/mcp-server/src/tools/register.ts - registering under `tool.title` with no uniqueness assertion and no hash over description and schema, explicitly with no poisoning found. Different file, different mechanism, no shared consequence.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Only that register.ts is the file that wires the token into the tools; that shared neighbourhood is not a shared defect, and the finding's own subject (name collisions and undetected definition drift) never touches the host/proxy path.

judgements.reason: Same files and the same class of flaw - unbounded model-supplied values forwarded unchanged into a credentialed job - but different parameters (`timeout`, `retryLimit`, `rateLimit`, `maxAllowedLimit`) reaching a different effect: quota burn and platform rate limiting for every consumer of the token, not exfiltration of the token itself.

Same file and same function (getHTMLFromAtext), but a different sink and a different context: the advisory is the HTML-attribute interpolation of `exportHtmlAdditionalTagsWithData` values into `span data-<k>="<v>"`, while F-001 is the author-colour value concatenated into the <style> block at line 95, which needs CSS validation and which the advisory's fix (Security.escapeHTMLAttribute on the hook name and value) would not repair.

Both are unescaped attribute writes in ExportHtml.ts reaching XSS in the export, but the tainted value differs: the advisory's is the pool value carried by the plugin hook, whereas F-002's is the author-derived class name passed only through stripDotFromAuthorID at emitOpenTag line 175 - and the advisory expressly notes that `author` attributes are the validated ones. Different source, different write site, and F-002 itself conditions the impact on that validation being defeatable.
judgements.what_would_settle_it: Whether an `author` pool value can actually diverge from a server-minted id; the advisory says it is validated, which is what keeps this a neighbouring sink rather than the same defect.

judgements.reason: Exactly the advisory's defect: line 66 builds `span data-${prop[0]}="${prop[1]}"` from the exportHtmlAdditionalTagsWithData hook output, core writes the quotes and escapes nothing, emitOpenTag emits the string raw, and a pool-controlled value containing a quote closes the attribute and yields stored XSS in the served export. Same hook, same line, same sink, same consequence, and the finding's fix is the same escaping the advisory applies (plus the sibling tag-name hook the advisory's fix also covers).

Same file, same function and the same missing HTML-attribute escaping, but at five different interpolation sites (lines 396-418) fed by a different pool value, `line.listTypeName` from the line's `list` attribute, on the plain export path with no plugin involved. Escaping the hook's name and value as the advisory does leaves these five sites unescaped, so it is a distinct sink rather than the advisory's defect narrowed.

The advisory is unescaped attribute-pool data reaching HTML export as stored XSS; F-005 is version disclosure through getPublicSettings() and the derived randomVersionString in src/node/utils/Settings.ts despite exposeVersion=false. Different file, different mechanism, different effect - information disclosure, not injection.

F-006 concerns the publicURL=null default in Settings.ts letting the request Host decide server-rendered absolute URLs in Open Graph metadata, a configuration-default and cache-poisoning issue. It shares neither the file, the tainted source (attribute pool), the sink (export HTML attribute) nor the outcome with the advisory's stored XSS.
